title: Tenses
examples: How do I know when to use the past continuous tense?
What is the difference between simple past and present perfect?
Can you give me an example of a future perfect tense?

explain.say: Today we are learning about verb tenses. Tenses help us show when an action happens.
The simple tense describes actions that are finished or happen regularly. For example, I walk to school every day.
The continuous tense shows an action happening right now or at a specific time. For example, she is reading a book at this moment.
The perfect tense connects two points in time using 'have' or 'has'. For example, I have eaten breakfast already this morning.
Let us look at the past perfect tense. This shows an action completed before another past action. For example, when he arrived, we had already left.

draw.text: Past Perfect: before another past time

explain.say: In real life, you use tenses when telling a story. If you say you played yesterday, you use the simple past tense.

faq.q: What is the difference between simple past and present perfect?
faq.a: Simple past describes a finished time, like yesterday. Present perfect connects the past to the present, like 'ever' or 'already'.
asks: When do I use 'did' versus 'have done'?

faq.q: How do I form the future continuous tense?
faq.a: You use 'will be' plus the verb ending in 'ing'. For example, I will be studying all afternoon.
asks: What is the structure for future continuous?
Can I use 'be' in the future continuous?

faq.q: When do I need the past perfect tense?
faq.a: You use it when one past action happened before another past action. It helps put events in the correct order.
asks: Is past perfect only for stories?

faq.q: Do all verbs change their tense?
faq.a: Yes, most verbs change. Some verbs, like 'is' or 'have', are helping verbs that help create the different tenses.

faq.q: Is the continuous tense always about 'right now'?
faq.a: No, it can show an action happening around a certain time in the past or future. For example, this time next week, I will be travelling.
asks: Can continuous be used for the future?

facts: Simple tenses use the base form or '-ed' ending.
Continuous tenses always use a form of 'to be' plus '-ing'.
The past perfect tense uses 'had' plus the past participle.
The simple present tense describes habits or facts.

quiz.why: Because 'last year' tells us the action is finished in the past, we use the simple past tense.

wrong.1: This is continuous, which suggests it is happening right now, not last year.
wrong.2: This is present perfect, which links to the present, but 'last year' sets it firmly in the past.
wrong.3: This is past perfect, which needs two past actions to compare, and we only have one time marker.

quiz.say: By the time the movie started, we (eat) all the popcorn.
quiz.show: By the time the movie started, we popcorn.
quiz.why: We use past perfect because eating the popcorn happened before the movie started in the past.

wrong.0: Simple past suggests the actions happened at the same time, which is not the order here.
wrong.1: Continuous suggests it is happening right now, not before the movie started.
wrong.2: Present perfect connects to the present, but the whole sentence is set in the past.

quiz.say: Tomorrow at this time, I (wait) for the bus.
quiz.show: Tomorrow at this time, I for the bus.
quiz.why: The structure 'will be + verb-ing' shows an action that will be in progress at a specific time in the future.

wrong.0: Simple future suggests a single point action, not an ongoing action at that time.
wrong.1: Past perfect is used for actions completed before another past time.
wrong.3: Simple present is for habits, not specific future moments.
